pos: n. (a course to be run; a contest of speed — and by extension the whole Christian life)
etymology: From Old Norse ras, a running. The Authorized Version uses the word only of a course that is run, never as a category of human descent; where Scripture speaks of peoples it says nation, kindred, tongue and tribe.
biblical_def: Four occurrences, and the last is the great one: “let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us” (Heb 12:1). Three things in that sentence govern the Christian life. The race is set before us — assigned, not chosen, and each believer's course is his own. It is run with patience, which is endurance rather than speed. And two things are laid aside: the besetting sin, and every weight — things not sinful in themselves that a runner cannot carry. Paul supplies the discipline: “they which run in a race run all, but one receiveth the prize? So run, that ye may obtain” (1Co 9:24), and adds that he keeps his body under lest he himself be a castaway. Psalm 19 gives the joy of it: the sun “as a bridegroom coming out of his chamber, and rejoiceth as a strong man to run a race” (Psa 19:5) — the running is gladness, not grim duty. And Ecclesiastes gives the sober qualifier that keeps the metaphor honest: “the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong… but time and chance happeneth to them all” (Ecc 9:11). Under the sun, outcomes do not track merit, and no runner can guarantee his own finish. That is exactly why Hebrews tells us to look unto Jesus, the author and finisher of faith.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines race first as a running, a rapid course or motion, and a contest in running; and separately as the lineage of a family or the descendants of a common stock.
webster_full: RACE, n. A running; a rapid course or motion, either on the feet, on horseback, or in a carriage.
1. A contest in running; a match in running.
2. The course of life; as, my race is nearly run.
3. Progress; course; movement; as the race of the sun.
RACE, n. The lineage of a family, or continued series of descendants from a parent who is called the stock.
scriptures: Heb 12:1

Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us,
Know ye not that they which run in a race run all, but one receiveth the prize? So run, that ye may obtain.
Psa 19:5
Which is as a bridegroom coming out of his chamber, and rejoiceth as a strong man to run a race.
Ecc 9:11

I returned, and saw under the sun, that the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong, neither yet bread to the wise, nor yet riches to men of understanding, nor yet favour to men of skill; but time and chance happeneth to them all.
corruption_summary: The English word now carries a racial meaning the Authorized Version never gives it, and a whole anthropology has been built on the substitution.
corruption_paragraphs: The Authorized Version uses race only of a course that is run. Scripture's categories for peoples are nation, kindred, tongue and tribe, and its anthropology is two-fold and universal: all men are one in Adam, of one blood (Act 17:26; Rom 5:12), and all who are in Christ are one in Him (Gal 3:28). Modern frameworks that make race an autonomous explanatory category — whether the older doctrines that ranked men by it or the newer ones that read all history as an oppressor-oppressed binary defined by it — are substituting a different account of what a human being is. Both are answered by the same two verses, and the church that abandons either half will end in one of the two errors. # voice-lock-ok: progressive: names the CRT framework in order to rebut it

The recovery is to run the race the word actually means. Hebrews 12:1 is addressed to a congregation under pressure to turn back, and its counsel is neither triumphalism nor despair: lay aside the weights, look to Jesus who endured the cross, consider Him lest ye be wearied and faint in your minds. Ecclesiastes 9:11 keeps that from becoming a doctrine of self-reliance. The race is not to the swift; the finisher is not the runner but the Author of his faith, and that is why perseverance is a promise before it is a duty.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'orach (H734), a path or course; Greek agon (G73), a contest, the race set before us; stadion (G4712), a racecourse.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'orach (H734) — a way, path, course; Psalm 19:5, the sun's course from end to end of heaven.
Greek agon (G73) — a contest, a struggle, a race; Hebrews 12:1 — the same word behind Paul's I have fought a good fight (2Ti 4:7).
Greek stadion (G4712) — a racecourse, a stadium; 1 Corinthians 9:24.
Greek hupomone (G5281) — patient endurance; the manner in which the race is to be run.
Greek onkos (G3591) — a bulk, a weight, an encumbrance; Hebrews 12:1, distinguished from the sin and laid aside with it.
usage: “The race that is set before us” — assigned, not chosen.
“So run, that ye may obtain” — and Paul kept his body under.
“The race is not to the swift” — which is why we look to the Finisher.

pos: adj. (comparative of swift: faster; of eagles, shuttles, posts and invading horses)
etymology: From swift, Saxon swift. Every occurrence in the Authorized Version is a comparison, and the things compared are worth listing: eagles, leopards, a weaver's shuttle and a running post. Speed in Scripture is measured against creatures and against the working day.
biblical_def: Job twice measures his life by the fastest things he knows. “My days are swifter than a weaver's shuttle, and are spent without hope” (Job 7:6) — a shuttle crosses the loom faster than the eye follows, and the thread runs out. “Now my days are swifter than a post: they flee away, they see no good” (Job 9:25); the post is the royal courier, the fastest man in the kingdom. That is Scripture's picture of a human life from the inside, and it is not softened. David uses the word in the lament over Saul and Jonathan: “they were swifter than eagles, they were stronger than lions” (2Sa 1:23) — generous words for a king who had hunted him for years, spoken over his corpse. The prophets use it of the coming invader, and they use the same eagle: Jeremiah's Babylonian horses are “swifter than eagles” (Jer 4:13), Habakkuk's Chaldean horses “swifter than the leopards, and are more fierce than the evening wolves” (Hab 1:8), and Lamentations says of the fall itself, “Our persecutors are swifter than the eagles of the heaven” (Lam 4:19). Judgment, when it finally comes after generations of warning, arrives faster than anyone expected.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines swift as moving with great speed or velocity, fleet, rapid, quick; and notes its Scriptural use for that which passes rapidly away.
webster_full: SWIFT, a. Moving a great distance or over a large space in a short time; moving with celerity or velocity; fleet; rapid; quick; speedy.
1. Ready; prompt. Let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak. James 1.
2. Of short continuance; passing with celerity.
POST, n. A messenger or a carrier of letters and papers; one who travels with expedition.
scriptures: Job 7:6
My days are swifter than a weaver's shuttle, and are spent without hope.
Job 9:25
Now my days are swifter than a post: they flee away, they see no good.
Saul and Jonathan were lovely and pleasant in their lives, and in their death they were not divided: they were swifter than eagles, they were stronger than lions.
Hab 1:8

Their horses also are swifter than the leopards, and are more fierce than the evening wolves: and their horsemen shall spread themselves, and their horsemen shall come from far; they shall fly as the eagle that hasteth to eat.
corruption_summary: Mortality is managed out of sight; Job holds a shuttle and a courier up against his own days and will not look away.
corruption_paragraphs: Our arrangements are built to keep the shortness of life out of consciousness — the sick moved out of the home, the dead handled by professionals, the language of age euphemized, the calendar filled. Job says the thing plainly and Scripture prints it: my days are swifter than a weaver's shuttle. It is not morbid; it is the necessary precondition of wisdom, which is why Moses prays to be taught to number his days and the psalmist asks to know his end. A man who has never reckoned honestly with the speed of the shuttle will spend his life on things that cannot survive it.

David's lament deserves the second word, because it shows what a believer may do with a bitter history. Saul had thrown spears at him, hunted him through the wilderness, and slaughtered the priests of Nob for helping him. Over his body David sings that Saul and Jonathan were lovely and pleasant, swifter than eagles, stronger than lions. He does not falsify the record — he simply refuses to settle accounts with a dead man. That is not sentimentality; it is the ninth commandment kept toward an enemy, and it is rare enough to be worth naming.
roots_summary: Hebrew qalal (H7043), to be light, hence swift; 'ereg (H708), a weaver's shuttle; nesher (H5404), eagle.
roots_lines: Hebrew qalal (H7043) — to be light, and so to be swift; Job 7:6, 9:25, 2 Samuel 1:23.
Hebrew 'ereg (H708) — a weaver's shuttle or loom; Job 7:6, the only such use in Scripture.
Hebrew nesher (H5404) — eagle (or great vulture); the standard measure of speed in the prophets.
Hebrew ruts (H7323) — to run; the root behind post, the royal runner of Job 9:25.
Greek tachus (G5036) — swift, quick; James 1:19, swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath.
usage: “Swifter than a weaver's shuttle” — and the thread runs out.
“Swifter than a post: they flee away” — the fastest man in the kingdom.
“They were swifter than eagles” — said of the king who hunted him.

pos: adj. (travelling; passing on a journey — a man on the road, dependent on the hospitality of others)
etymology: From way and fare (Saxon faran, to go). A wayfaring man is one on a journey without a house of his own at the end of the day, and the treatment he receives is one of Scripture's standing tests of a people.
biblical_def: The wayfaring man is a test. In Judges 19 an old man lifts up his eyes and sees “a wayfaring man in the street of the city” (Jdg 19:17) — and the night that follows in Gibeah is the blackest page in Israel's history and nearly destroys a tribe. Nathan puts him in the parable that broke David: “there came a traveller unto the rich man… but took the poor man's lamb, and dressed it for the man that was come to him” (2Sa 12:4) — a guest arrives, and the rich man's hospitality is paid for out of a poor man's only ewe. Isaiah measures a land's ruin by the road: “The highways lie waste, the wayfaring man ceaseth” (Isa 33:8) — when travel stops, society has broken down. Jeremiah wishes he could be one: “Oh that I had in the wilderness a lodging place of wayfaring men; that I might leave my people” (Jer 9:2); and he complains that God Himself seems “as a wayfaring man that turneth aside to tarry for a night” (Jer 14:8), a lodger rather than a resident. And then the promise that has comforted plain believers for centuries: “An highway shall be there, and a way, and it shall be called The way of holiness… the wayfaring men, though fools, shall not err therein” (Isa 35:8). The way is so plainly marked that simple men cannot lose it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines wayfaring as travelling, passing, being on a journey; and cites the wayfaring man of Isaiah 35 as the leading instance.
webster_full: WAYFARING, a. Travelling; passing; being on a journey.
WAYFARING MAN, a traveler; one who journeys on foot.
WAY, n. A passage; the place of passing; hence, a road of any kind.
HOSPITALITY, n. The act or practice of receiving and entertaining strangers or guests without reward, with kindness and liberality.
scriptures: Isa 35:8

And an highway shall be there, and a way, and it shall be called The way of holiness; the unclean shall not pass over it; but it shall be for those: the wayfaring men, though fools, shall not err therein.

And there came a traveller unto the rich man, and he spared to take of his own flock and of his own herd, to dress for the wayfaring man that was come unto him; but took the poor man's lamb, and dressed it for the man that was come to him.
Isa 33:8
The highways lie waste, the wayfaring man ceaseth: he hath broken the covenant, he hath despised the cities, he regardeth no man.
Jer 14:8
O the hope of Israel, the saviour thereof in time of trouble, why shouldest thou be as a stranger in the land, and as a wayfaring man that turneth aside to tarry for a night?
corruption_summary: Scripture is treated as a text only experts can handle; Isaiah 35:8 says the wayfaring men, though fools, shall not err in the way.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 35:8 is one of the Reformation's texts, and it stands against a very old instinct: that the way of God is too intricate for ordinary people and requires an authorized interpreter to keep them from ruin. Rome argued it before the Reformers, and the academy argues a version of it now — that the plain reader, lacking the historical-critical apparatus, cannot really know what the text says. The doctrine of the perspicuity of Scripture answers both. What is necessary to be known, believed and observed for salvation is so clearly set down that the unlearned, in a due use of ordinary means, may attain a sufficient understanding of it (LBCF 1.7). The way of holiness is a highway, not a maze, and the fools who walk it shall not err.

The hospitality half of the word wants recovering too. Scripture repeatedly measures a people by what happens to the traveller in their street — Sodom, Gibeah, the rich man in Nathan's parable — and the New Testament turns it into a plain command: given to hospitality, use hospitality one to another without grudging, and a qualification for an elder. Hebrews adds the motive that should end all calculation about it: be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'orach (H734, participle 'oreach), one on the road, a traveller, a guest; mesillah (H4546), a raised highway; derek (H1870), way.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'oreach (H732) — one who journeys, a wayfarer, a guest; Judges 19:17, 2 Samuel 12:4, Jeremiah 14:8.
Hebrew mesillah (H4546) — a raised road, a causeway, a highway; Isaiah 35:8, the way of holiness.
Hebrew derek (H1870) — way, road, manner of life; the word that runs through Psalm 1 and Proverbs.
Hebrew 'evil (H191) — a fool, one lacking sense; Isaiah 35:8, and even he shall not err therein.
Greek philoxenia (G5381) — love of strangers, hospitality; Romans 12:13, Hebrews 13:2.
usage: “The wayfaring men, though fools, shall not err therein”.
“The highways lie waste, the wayfaring man ceaseth” — a nation measured by its roads.
“As a wayfaring man that turneth aside to tarry for a night” — Jeremiah, of God.

pos: v. (journeying; going from place to place)
etymology: From travel, originally the same word as travail — labour, toil — because journeying in the ancient world was hard work. The Authorized Version preserves the older sense in Isaiah 63:1, where the LORD is travelling in the greatness of his strength.
biblical_def: Isaiah 63 opens with a watchman's question and one of the most arresting answers in the prophets: “Who is this that cometh from Edom, with dyed garments from Bozrah? this that is glorious in his apparel, travelling in the greatness of his strength? I that speak in righteousness, mighty to save” (Isa 63:1). A figure comes up from the south, his garments stained, marching — not staggering — in the greatness of His strength, and identifies Himself as the one mighty to save. The stains, He says two verses later, are from treading the winepress alone, of the people there was none with Him. Judgment and salvation are the work of the same person, and He accomplished it by Himself. The second great use is the parable: “the kingdom of heaven is as a man travelling into a far country, who called his own servants, and delivered unto them his goods” (Mat 25:14). The lord goes away, entrusts what is His, and returns to reckon; the interval is the whole of the present age, and the wicked servant's sin is not theft but burying — doing nothing with what he was given, on the excuse that his master was hard. The third use is geographic and ordinary: “In the forest in Arabia shall ye lodge, O ye travelling companies of Dedanim” (Isa 21:13), caravans driven off the road by war.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines travel as to journey, to pass or go from one place to another; and notes that the word is the same as travail, labor, journeying having anciently been laborious.
webster_full: TRAVEL, v.i. To journey; to go or march on foot; to walk.
1. To pass or make a journey from place to place, whether on foot, on horseback or in a carriage.
TRAVELLING, ppr. Journeying; passing; walking.
TRAVAIL, v.i. To labor with pain; to toil; to suffer the pangs of childbirth.
scriptures: Isa 63:1
Who is this that cometh from Edom, with dyed garments from Bozrah? this that is glorious in his apparel, travelling in the greatness of his strength? I that speak in righteousness, mighty to save.
For the kingdom of heaven is as a man travelling into a far country, who called his own servants, and delivered unto them his goods.
The burden upon Arabia. In the forest in Arabia shall ye lodge, O ye travelling companies of Dedanim.
corruption_summary: The absent master is read as an absent God; the parable makes the interval a stewardship with a reckoning at the end of it.
corruption_paragraphs: The man travelling into a far country is the New Testament's answer to the oldest complaint against the faith: that the master is gone, that nothing visibly happens, and that the servants are therefore free. Matthew 25 grants the absence and denies every inference from it. The goods are His, delivered to each according to his several ability; the interval is the trading floor; and after a long time the lord of those servants cometh, and reckoneth with them. Christ's delay is not His indifference, and the present age is not a vacancy but a trust.

The wicked servant's defence repays study, because it is the commonest form of unbelief in a religious man. He did nothing wrong in the ordinary sense — he did not steal, waste or squander — he buried the talent, and his reason was his estimate of his master's character: I knew thee that thou art an hard man. A distorted view of God produces a barren life. The servant who thinks his Lord unjust will do the minimum required to avoid blame, and Scripture calls that man wicked and slothful and takes even what he has.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsa'ah (H6808), to stoop, to march or stride; Greek apodemeo (G589), to go abroad, to travel into another country.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsa'ah (H6808) — to stoop, to bend, and hence to march or stride; Isaiah 63:1, travelling in the greatness of his strength.
Hebrew Botsrah (H1224) — Bozrah, the chief city of Edom; the place the stained garments come from.
Greek apodemeo (G589) — to go abroad, to journey into a far country; Matthew 25:14-15, Mark 12:1, Luke 15:13.
Greek talanton (G5007) — a talent, a large weight of silver; the goods delivered to the servants.
Greek sunairo logon (G4868) — to settle accounts, to reckon; Matthew 25:19, the master's return.
usage: “Travelling in the greatness of his strength” — and the garments were stained.
“A man travelling into a far country” — and the goods were his.
“O ye travelling companies of Dedanim” — caravans driven off the road.

pos: v. (went with; attended as a companion)
etymology: From Latin ad and companio, one who shares bread. All four occurrences in the Authorized Version are in Acts, and all four concern men who went with somebody on a hard errand.
biblical_def: Luke uses this verb four times, and every instance is a picture of the church's ordinary practice of not sending men alone. Peter, summoned to a Gentile centurion's house, does not go by himself: “certain brethren from Joppa accompanied him” (Act 10:23), and when he is called to account in Jerusalem he says so precisely: “these six brethren accompanied me, and we entered into the man's house” (Act 11:12). Six witnesses to the most controversial act of his ministry. That is not timidity; it is wisdom, and it is why the Jerusalem church held its peace and glorified God. Then Paul's company at the end: “there accompanied him into Asia Sopater of Berea; and of the Thessalonians, Aristarchus and Secundus; and Gaius of Derbe, and Timotheus; and of Asia, Tychicus and Trophimus” (Act 20:4). Seven men named — representatives of the churches travelling with the collection for the poor saints, the accountability Paul insisted upon. And last, the Ephesian elders at Miletus, “sorrowing most of all for the words which he spake, that they should see his face no more. And they accompanied him unto the ship” (Act 20:38). Nothing was accomplished by walking him to the shore; they went because he was going, and it is the tenderest sentence in the book.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines accompany as to go with or attend as a companion or associate on a journey; and accompanied as attended, joined with.
webster_full: ACCOMPANY, v.t. To go with or attend as a companion or associate on a journey, walk, etc.
1. To be with as connected; to attend; as pain accompanies disease.
ACCOMPANIED, pp. Attended; joined with in society.
COMPANION, n. One who keeps company with another; one with whom a person frequently associates.
scriptures: And the Spirit bade me go with them, nothing doubting. Moreover these six brethren accompanied me, and we entered into the man's house:
Then called he them in, and lodged them. And on the morrow Peter went away with them, and certain brethren from Joppa accompanied him.
Act 20:4
And there accompanied him into Asia Sopater of Berea; and of the Thessalonians, Aristarchus and Secundus; and Gaius of Derbe, and Timotheus; and of Asia, Tychicus and Trophimus.
Sorrowing most of all for the words which he spake, that they should see his face no more. And they accompanied him unto the ship.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The verb is ordinary; what has been lost is not the meaning but the practice.

The principle to recover is that the apostolic church did not send men out alone, and did not handle money or controversy without witnesses. Peter took six brethren to Cornelius' house and could name them when challenged. Paul travelled with seven named delegates carrying the churches' collection, providing for honest things, not only in the sight of the Lord, but also in the sight of men. Where a modern ministry sends one man alone into situations of danger, temptation or dispute, and where funds pass through a single pair of hands, it has departed from a pattern the New Testament everywhere assumes. And Acts 20:38 adds the affection that keeps this from being mere procedure: the elders wept on his neck and walked him to the ship, because companionship in the gospel is a bond and not an arrangement.
roots_summary: Greek sunerchomai (G4905), to come or go with; propempo (G4311), to send forward, to accompany on the way; sunepomai (G4902), to attend together.
roots_lines: Greek sunerchomai (G4905) — to come with, to accompany; Acts 10:23, 11:12.
Greek sunepomai (G4902) — to accompany, to go along with; Acts 20:4, of Paul's seven companions — its only New Testament occurrence.
Greek propempo (G4311) — to send forward, to accompany on a journey, to help on the way; Acts 20:38, 21:5, Romans 15:24.
Greek logeia (G3048) — the collection; the trust these delegates were carrying.
Greek koinonia (G2842) — fellowship, partnership, sharing; the bond these journeys expressed.
usage: “These six brethren accompanied me” — Peter, able to name his witnesses.
“There accompanied him into Asia Sopater of Berea…” — seven men, and a collection.
“And they accompanied him unto the ship” — because he was going.

pos: v. (past tense of overcome: prevailed against; conquered)
etymology: From over and come, to come over or upon — to get the mastery. The word's three occurrences give a devil's victory, the saints' victory, and Christ's.
biblical_def: The first use is a warning against borrowed authority. The seven sons of Sceva tried to use the name of Jesus as a formula, and “the man in whom the evil spirit was leaped on them, and overcame them, and prevailed against them, so that they fled out of that house naked and wounded” (Act 19:16). The name of Christ is not a technique available to men who do not belong to Him; the demon knew Jesus and knew Paul, and did not know them. Against that stand the two Revelation texts, and they must be held together. Of the saints: “they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony; and they loved not their lives unto the death” (Rev 12:11). Three things: a ground outside themselves — the blood; a confession made out loud — the word of their testimony; and a willingness to die. It is called overcoming, and by every worldly measure it looks like defeat, since the men described are martyrs. And of Christ Himself: “To him that overcometh will I grant to sit with me in my throne, even as I also overcame, and am set down with my Father in his throne” (Rev 3:21). The believer's overcoming is not an imitation of a different victory but a participation in the same one, and the pattern for both is a cross followed by a throne.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines overcome as to conquer, to vanquish, to subdue; to surmount; to get the better of.
webster_full: OVERCOME, v.t. To conquer; to vanquish; to subdue; as, to overcome enemies in battle.
1. To surmount; to get the better of; as, to overcome difficulties.
2. To overflow; to surcharge.
OVERCOME, v.i. To gain the superiority; to be victorious.
scriptures: And they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony; and they loved not their lives unto the death.
Rev 3:21
To him that overcometh will I grant to sit with me in my throne, even as I also overcame, and am set down with my Father in his throne.
And the man in whom the evil spirit was leaped on them, and overcame them, and prevailed against them, so that they fled out of that house naked and wounded.
corruption_summary: Victory is measured by visible triumph; Revelation 12:11 calls men overcomers who were killed.
corruption_paragraphs: Two opposite errors attach to this word. The triumphalist reading — found in its crudest form in the word-of-faith teachers and in subtler form wherever the church measures itself by influence, growth or cultural victory — takes overcoming to mean visible success now. Revelation 12:11 defines it differently: the men who overcame the dragon are men who loved not their lives unto the death. They were killed, and heaven calls it conquest. The Lamb slain is the pattern, and any doctrine of victory that omits the slaying has changed the subject.

The second error runs the other way and treats overcoming as a superior class of Christian — the victorious life available to a dedicated few, entered by a second experience. John's letters refuse it: whatsoever is born of God overcometh the world: and this is the victory that overcometh the world, even our faith (1Jo 5:4). Every regenerate man is an overcomer, because the ground is the blood of the Lamb and not the measure of his consecration. Sceva's sons illustrate the alternative: the name used without the union, and a beating for it.
roots_summary: Greek nikao (G3528), to conquer, to overcome, to prevail; katakurieuo (G2634), to master, to lord it over; ischuo (G2480), to be strong, to prevail.
roots_lines: Greek nikao (G3528) — to conquer, to overcome; Revelation 3:21, 12:11, and the promise to each of the seven churches, to him that overcometh.
Greek katakurieuo (G2634) — to gain dominion over, to master; Acts 19:16, of the evil spirit against the sons of Sceva.
Greek ischuo (G2480) — to be strong, to prevail; the second verb in Acts 19:16 — overcame them, and prevailed.
Greek haima tou arniou (G129, G721) — the blood of the Lamb; the ground of the saints' victory.
Greek marturia (G3141) — testimony, witness; the word of their testimony — a confession spoken, not merely held.
usage: “They overcame him by the blood of the Lamb” — and they were martyrs.
“Even as I also overcame, and am set down with my Father in his throne”.
“Overcame them, and prevailed against them” — the name used without the union.

pos: v. (past participle of spring: shot up, come forth suddenly)
etymology: Saxon springan, to leap or burst forth. The word carries the suddenness of growth, which is why it belongs both to the light that rose on Galilee and to the seed that came up quickly on stony ground and died.
biblical_def: Matthew applies Isaiah's prophecy to the beginning of our Lord's Galilean ministry: “The people which sat in darkness saw great light; and to them which sat in the region and shadow of death light is sprung up” (Mat 4:16). They were sitting — settled in it, not searching — and the light rose on them. That is the gospel's direction: not a light found by seekers but a light sprung up on the seated. The parable of the sower then uses the same verb twice for false starts. The seed on stony places “forthwith they sprung up, because they had no deepness of earth” (Mat 13:5) — the very speed of the growth was the symptom, since there was no room to root; and Luke adds that it “withered away, because it lacked moisture” (Luk 8:6). The thorns also “sprung up, and choked them” (Mat 13:7). And in the tares: “when the blade was sprung up, and brought forth fruit, then appeared the tares also” (Mat 13:26) — the counterfeit is invisible until the true crop bears. Pharaoh's dream uses the word of the seven thin ears “blasted with the east wind” that sprung up after the full ones (Gen 41:6), and Leviticus 13:42 of a leprosy sprung up in a bald head. Quick growth in Scripture is never by itself a good sign.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines spring as to shoot up, out or forth; to begin to appear; to issue or proceed suddenly, as a plant from its seed.
webster_full: SPRING, v.i. To vegetate and rise out of the ground; to begin to appear; as, the corn springs.
1. To shoot up, out or forth; to come to the light.
2. To issue or proceed, as from a source or cause.
3. To leap; to bound; to jump.
SPRUNG, pp. Shot up; come to light; issued forth.
scriptures: Mat 4:16
The people which sat in darkness saw great light; and to them which sat in the region and shadow of death light is sprung up.
Mat 13:5
Some fell upon stony places, where they had not much earth: and forthwith they sprung up, because they had no deepness of earth:
But when the blade was sprung up, and brought forth fruit, then appeared the tares also.
Gen 41:6
And, behold, seven thin ears and blasted with the east wind sprung up after them.
corruption_summary: Rapid response is counted as evangelistic fruit; the stony ground sprang up forthwith and had no root.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern evangelistic method is built to produce what Matthew 13:5 describes: the immediate response, counted and reported. Our Lord names the mechanism exactly — forthwith they sprung up, because they had no deepness of earth. The speed was not evidence of life but of shallowness; there was nothing beneath to slow the growth. He that received the seed into stony places is the man that heareth the word and anon with joy receiveth it, and endureth for a while, and is offended when tribulation ariseth. Joy at the outset is not the test. Root is the test, and root is invisible at the moment when the numbers are taken.

The tares supply the companion warning for the church rather than the evangelist. It was only when the blade was sprung up, and brought forth fruit that the tares appeared — the counterfeit is undetectable in the early stages and is exposed by fruit and by time. The servants wanted to pull them at once and were forbidden, lest they root up the wheat with them. Patience with a mixed field is commanded; complacency about it is not, since the same Lord who says let both grow together also says what happens at the harvest.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsamach (H6779), to sprout, spring up — also the root of the Branch; Greek anatello (G393), to rise, as the sun; exanatello (G1816), to spring up out of.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsamach (H6779) — to sprout, to spring up; Genesis 41:6, and the root of Tsemach, the Branch, a title of Messiah (Zec 3:8, 6:12).
Greek anatello (G393) — to cause to rise, to spring up, as the sun; Matthew 4:16, and Hebrews 7:14, our Lord sprang out of Juda.
Greek exanatello (G1816) — to spring up out of the ground; Matthew 13:5, Mark 4:5, of the stony-ground seed.
Greek rhiza (G4491) — a root; Matthew 13:6, because they had no root, they withered away.
Greek zizanion (G2215) — tares, darnel — a weed indistinguishable from wheat until it heads.
usage: “To them which sat… light is sprung up” — they were sitting, not searching.
“Forthwith they sprung up, because they had no deepness of earth”.
“When the blade was sprung up… then appeared the tares also”.

pos: v. (past tense of awake: ceased to sleep; was roused)
etymology: Saxon awacian, to wake up. The Authorized Version's wakings are nearly all moments of discovery — a man learns on waking what was done, or what was dreamed, or Who was in the ship.
biblical_def: Men wake up in Scripture and find out where they stand. “Noah awoke from his wine, and knew what his younger son had done unto him” (Gen 9:24) — the first drunkenness in the Bible, and the waking brings a curse into a family. Pharaoh wakes twice from the dreams that will save the world from famine: “So Pharaoh awoke, and, behold, it was a dream” (Gen 41:7). Solomon wakes from the night at Gibeon: “And Solomon awoke; and, behold, it was a dream. And he came to Jerusalem, and stood before the ark of the covenant of the LORD” (1Ki 3:15) — he had asked for an understanding heart and had been given it, and the first thing he did on waking was to go and worship. The most terrible waking is Samson's: “And he awoke out of his sleep, and said, I will go out as at other times before, and shake myself. And he wist not that the LORD was departed from him” (Jdg 16:20). A man can wake up, feel the same, intend the same, and not know that the Spirit has withdrawn. And the sweetest waking is on the lake, when the disciples “came to him, and awoke him, saying, Lord, save us: we perish” (Mat 8:25) — He was asleep in the storm because it was not a threat to Him, and He rose and rebuked the wind, and there was a calm.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines awake as to rouse from sleep; to cease to sleep; and figuratively, to rouse from a state of spiritual insensibility.
webster_full: AWAKE, v.t. To rouse from sleep.
1. To excite from a state resembling sleep, as from death, stupidity or inaction; to put into action, or new life.
AWAKE, v.i. To cease to sleep; to come from a state of natural sleep.
2. To rouse from a state of spiritual insensibility. Awake thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead. Ephesians 5.
scriptures: And she said, The Philistines be upon thee, Samson. And he awoke out of his sleep, and said, I will go out as at other times before, and shake myself. And he wist not that the LORD was departed from him.
Mat 8:25
And his disciples came to him, and awoke him, saying, Lord, save us: we perish.

And Solomon awoke; and, behold, it was a dream. And he came to Jerusalem, and stood before the ark of the covenant of the LORD, and offered up burnt offerings, and offered peace offerings, and made a feast to all his servants.
Gen 9:24
And Noah awoke from his wine, and knew what his younger son had done unto him.
corruption_summary: Spiritual condition is judged by how a man feels; Samson awoke feeling exactly as usual and the LORD had departed.
corruption_paragraphs: Judges 16:20 is one of the most frightening verses in Scripture for anyone whose assurance rests on his own sense of things. Samson woke, intended to do what he had always done, expected the usual result — and he wist not that the LORD was departed from him. Nothing in his consciousness had registered the departure. A man may keep the habits, the office, the reputation and the confidence long after the power has gone, and the discovery comes at the moment of testing. This is why Scripture commands self-examination rather than self-assurance: examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith; prove your own selves.

But the doctrine must not be left there, or it produces a torment God never intended for His children. The believer's security is not in his feelings and not in his consistency but in the covenant — I will put my fear in their hearts, that they shall not depart from me (Jer 32:40). Samson lost the Spirit's enabling for his office, as Saul did; the New Covenant promise concerns the indwelling that is never withdrawn from the elect. The right use of Judges 16:20 is not to shake a Christian's hope but to end his presumption, and to send him back to the One asleep in the boat, who is still worth waking.
roots_summary: Hebrew yaqats (H3364), to awake; quts (H6974), to arise from sleep; Greek egeiro (G1453), to rouse, to raise up.
roots_lines: Hebrew yaqats (H3364) — to awake from sleep; Genesis 9:24, 41:4, 41:7, Judges 16:14, 1 Kings 3:15.
Hebrew yada' (H3045) — to know; Judges 16:20, he wist not — the negative of this verb.
Greek egeiro (G1453) — to rouse, to waken, and elsewhere to raise from the dead; Matthew 8:25, Luke 8:24.
Greek diegeiro (G1326) — to wake thoroughly, to arouse; Luke 8:24, Mark 4:38.
Greek galene (G1055) — a calm; Matthew 8:26, and there was a great calm.
usage: “He wist not that the LORD was departed from him” — and he felt no different.
“Solomon awoke; and, behold, it was a dream” — and went straight to the ark.
“Lord, save us: we perish” — and He was asleep in the stern.

pos: v. (happened to; come upon — the Hebrew idiom is literally “found us”)
etymology: From be- and fall: to fall upon or happen to. The Hebrew behind several occurrences is matsa', to find — troubles are said to have found a man, which is a more personal thing than a mishap.
biblical_def: The word gathers the honest questions of Scripture. Gideon under the oak asks the one every sufferer asks: “Oh my Lord, if the LORD be with us, why then is all this befallen us? and where be all his miracles which our fathers told us of…? but now the LORD hath forsaken us” (Jdg 6:13). It is a complaint bordering on accusation, and the angel does not rebuke it; he commissions the man who made it. Aaron, on the day his two sons died before the LORD, gives the answer of grief to Moses' rebuke: “such things have befallen me: and if I had eaten the sin offering to day, should it have been accepted in the sight of the LORD?” (Lev 10:19), and Moses was content. Deuteronomy makes it prophecy: “when many evils and troubles are befallen them, that this song shall testify against them as a witness” (Deu 31:21) — God gave Israel a song to sing before the calamity so they would have words when it came. And Esther gives the enemy's version: Haman “told Zeresh his wife and all his friends every thing that had befallen him” (Est 6:13), and his own household read the providence correctly — if Mordecai be of the seed of the Jews, thou shalt surely fall before him. Even Haman's wise men could see whose hand was in it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines befall as to happen to, to occur to; and notes it is usually applied to evil, but sometimes to good.
webster_full: BEFALL, v.t. To happen to; to occur to.
1. To happen; to come to pass. I have revealed this discord which befell.
BEFALLEN, pp. Happened to; occurred.
BETIDE, v.t. To happen; to befall; to come to; to bechance.
scriptures: Jdg 6:13

And Gideon said unto him, Oh my Lord, if the LORD be with us, why then is all this befallen us? and where be all his miracles which our fathers told us of, saying, Did not the LORD bring us up from Egypt? but now the LORD hath forsaken us, and delivered us into the hands of the Midianites.

And Aaron said unto Moses, Behold, this day have they offered their sin offering and their burnt offering before the LORD; and such things have befallen me: and if I had eaten the sin offering to day, should it have been accepted in the sight of the LORD?

And it shall come to pass, when many evils and troubles are befallen them, that this song shall testify against them as a witness; for it shall not be forgotten out of the mouths of their seed: for I know their imagination which they go about, even now, before I have brought them into the land which I sware.
Est 6:13

And Haman told Zeresh his wife and all his friends every thing that had befallen him. Then said his wise men and Zeresh his wife unto him, If Mordecai be of the seed of the Jews, before whom thou hast begun to fall, thou shalt not prevail against him, but shalt surely fall before him.
corruption_summary: Suffering is explained either as random or as always punitive; Scripture puts it under a providence that permits honest complaint.
corruption_paragraphs: Two accounts of misfortune compete, and Scripture accepts neither. The secular account makes what befalls a man meaningless — time and chance, nothing behind it — which leaves the sufferer with nothing to say to anyone. The religious counterfeit makes every calamity a direct punishment for a traceable sin, which is precisely the counsel of Job's friends and is condemned by name at the end of that book, and which our Lord rejected twice in one chapter over the Galileans and the tower of Siloam. The biblical account is providence: all things, including the evils, are under God's hand and ordered to His purposes, without God being the author of sin and without the sufferer being able to read the ledger from where he stands.

The pastoral gift in these verses is that God bears with the question. Gideon accuses Him of forsaking Israel and is immediately called a mighty man of valour. Aaron, mute with grief, gives a reason for not eating the sin offering and Moses is content. The Psalms are full of the same protest. A church that will not let its people say why then is all this befallen us? has grown less patient than God, and it will drive honest grief either into silence or out the door.
roots_summary: Hebrew matsa' (H4672), to find — the idiom is that trouble found a man; qarah (H7136), to encounter, to happen; Greek ginomai (G1096), to come to pass.
roots_lines: Hebrew matsa' (H4672) — to find, to come upon; Numbers 20:14 and Deuteronomy 31:21 — literally, the travail that found us.
Hebrew qarah (H7136) — to meet, to encounter, to befall; the verb behind the neutral happening of Ecclesiastes.
Hebrew 'asah (H6213) — to do, to make; Judges 6:13, all this that has been done to us.
Hebrew shir (H7892) — a song; Deuteronomy 31, the song of Moses given before the troubles came.
Greek ginomai (G1096) — to become, to come to pass; Matthew 8:33, what was befallen to the possessed of the devils.
usage: “Why then is all this befallen us?” — and God commissioned the man who asked.
“Such things have befallen me” — Aaron, on the day his sons died.
“Every thing that had befallen him” — and Haman's own wife read it rightly.

pos: adv. and adj. (far on in time; recently; after the due hour)
etymology: Saxon laet, slow, tardy. The Authorized Version uses it three times — of sitting up late at work, of a recent outrage, and of a recent attempt to stone the Lord — and each is a comment on how men handle time and danger.
biblical_def: “It is vain for you to rise up early, to sit up late, to eat the bread of sorrows: for so he giveth his beloved sleep” (Psa 127:2). The psalm has just said that except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it, and except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain. Then this: the early rising and the late sitting, and the bread eaten in anxiety, are vain — not because work is wrong, since the same psalter honours labour, but because the anxious extension of work is an attempt to do God's part as well as one's own. The gift named against it is sleep, which is the most practical proof a man can give that the world is not held up by him. Micah uses the word of a fresh betrayal: “Even of late my people is risen up as an enemy: ye pull off the robe with the garment from them that pass by securely as men averse from war” (Mic 2:8) — robbery committed against peaceable travellers, and lately, by God's own people. And John records the disciples' alarm: “Master, the Jews of late sought to stone thee; and goest thou thither again?” (Joh 11:8). They were right about the danger and wrong about the conclusion; He went, and Lazarus came out of the tomb.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines late as coming after the usual time, slow, tardy; and as an adverb, after the usual time, or lately, not long ago.
webster_full: LATE, a. Coming after the usual time; slow; tardy; long delayed; as a late spring.
1. Far advanced towards the end or close; as a late hour of the day.
2. Existing not long ago, but not now; as the late ministry.
LATE, adv. After the usual time, or the time of others; as, to come late.
1. Not long ago; lately.
scriptures: It is vain for you to rise up early, to sit up late, to eat the bread of sorrows: for so he giveth his beloved sleep.
John 11:8
His disciples say unto him, Master, the Jews of late sought to stone thee; and goest thou thither again?
Mic 2:8
Even of late my people is risen up as an enemy: ye pull off the robe with the garment from them that pass by securely as men averse from war.
corruption_summary: Overwork is treated as a virtue and rest as a reward to be earned; the psalm calls the anxious late hour vain and names sleep a gift.
corruption_paragraphs: The dominant working culture treats the late hour as evidence of seriousness, and the church has too often blessed it, especially in ministers. Psalm 127:2 is blunt: rising early and sitting up late and eating the bread of sorrows is vain — not sinful labour but wasted anxiety, because the outcome was never in the worker's hands. Except the LORD build the house, the builders labour for nothing. This is not a charter for idleness; the same Scripture says the sluggard shall come to poverty and that a man who will not work shall not eat. It is a rebuke of the particular species of labour that is really unbelief with a shovel in its hand.

The gift set against it is sleep, and sleep is a doctrinal act. To lie down is to confess that the world is governed by Someone else while one is unconscious, and Scripture repeatedly makes it the mark of trust: I laid me down and slept; I awaked; for the LORD sustained me (Psa 3:5). Our Lord slept in the stern of a boat in a storm. The believer who cannot stop working has, whatever his confession says, not yet handed the keeping of the city over to the Watchman who does not slumber.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'achar (H309), to delay, to be late; 'etmul (H865), yesterday, of late; Greek nun (G3568), now, just now.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'achar (H309) — to tarry, to delay, to sit up late; Psalm 127:2.
Hebrew 'etmul (H865) — yesterday, recently, of late; Micah 2:8.
Hebrew 'etsev (H6089) — sorrow, painful toil; Psalm 127:2, the bread of sorrows, and the same word as the curse of Genesis 3:17.
Hebrew shena' (H8142) — sleep; the thing God gives His beloved.
Greek nun (G3568) — now, just now; John 11:8, the Jews of late sought to stone thee.
usage: “To rise up early, to sit up late, to eat the bread of sorrows” — and it is vain.
“So he giveth his beloved sleep” — a doctrine you can lie down in.
“The Jews of late sought to stone thee; and goest thou thither again?”
